newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - UK public sector pay could prompt tax rises.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - UK public sector pay could prompt tax rises.

text.p: An unexpectedly large pay bill for Britain's 1.3 million public sector workers could threaten the government's tight spending targets and lead to tax rises after the election if savings cannot be found elsewhere.

But with opposition Labour well ahead in the opinion polls, analysts said on Friday it is more likely to be a thorny problem for shadow finance spokesman Gordon Brown to solve than Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke.

The Financial Times newspaper reported on Friday that five independent pay review bodies have recommended doctors, teachers and the armed forces receive pay rises of between 3.2 and 3.4 percent, well above what government spending plans can meet.

Clarke -- conscious of the need to to ease the pressure on tight budgets, particularly in the health service -- is expected to phase in the awards in stages, gambling that workers will be placated by the relatively high overall increase.
The cabinet will meet to discuss the pay deal next Thursday.

Speaking at a Conservative Central Office, Prime Minister John Major said: "We will be putting the pay review reports to Cabinet next Thursday. Until we have discussed them and made our decisions in Cabinet, I am not going to anticipate what the outcome will be."
Meanwhile, Labour's Brown told a conference in London that a future Labour government would take a firm approach to public sector pay, and settlements would have to be made within tough cash limits.
He said all public sector pay agreements would have to be financed from within the agreed departmental cash limits upon which departments now plan. There would be no "blank cheques."
If the government accepted the pay recommendation it could mean one of two things -- higher taxes or further cuts and job losses in the public sector.

"Many people were concerned the government would fail to meet its spending targets, especially since public sector pay has been repressed for so long," said Martin Weale, head of the National Institute of Economic Research and one of the Treasury's independent advisers.
In his November budget, Clarke cut planned spending to compensate for a one penny reduction in income tax.
"This pay round just strengthens the argument that taxes will have to rise after the election," Weale said.

The election has to be called by May and the latest poll from the MORI organisation shows the Labour Party enjoying a 25 point lead, so the tax problem is likely to land firmly at Gordon Brown's door.
"There is a good chance that it won't be Clarke who has to find the cash from somewhere else," said Alissa Goodman, research economist at the Institute for Fiscal Studies.
Brown has pledged not to change the key rates of income tax but there are plenty of other options open to him.
Weale said national insurance, corporation tax and personal allowances could all be fiddled with.
The alternative would be cuts in the public sector. Already for the past four years, the government has ruled that public sector pay rises had to be matched by savings elsewhere.
